PLANT THE MOON CHALLENGE
FINAL REPORT
Wirt County High School
Team Name: Wirt Astro Tigers
2023-2024

Introduction
Background Information/Planning
At the start of brainstorming, our team decided to compile a few leading questions and
experiment criteria that would lead the entirety of the experiment. First, we deduced we
would need to find a plant that is resistant to change, grows quickly, and acts as a
nutritious food source. These were the criteria that we chose because we felt that they
would help the plant grow and/or bloom within the time frame we were given. After
some research, we found a variety of pea called the Organic Patio Pride Pea that would
meet the prior criteria well. (See “Dependent Variables” for more information on the
Patio Pride Pea)
Next, we knew we needed to decide what factors we were going to test and came to the
conclusion that the main focus of our experiment would be on what soil additives are the
lightest weight and have the best nutrition for Patio Pride Peas when in collaboration
with lunar regolith. All of our soil additive decisions stem from the goal of keeping things
as lightweight as possible while still being effective in growing healthy peas. (See
“Independent Variables” for more information on the chosen soil additives)
Alongside the soil additives, our team chose a watering and lighting procedure for the
growth of our plants. For the light, we chose to utilize a plant grow light that all of the
plants would be placed under so that the light was constantly consistent. For our
watering procedure, we chose to base our water amount off of the individual plant’s
moisture level, rather than giving all plants the same amount. This ensured that we
would not end up having some plants with a good amount of water and some plants that
are waterlogged.
Lastly, we decided what factors we would introduce and measure in order to record the
effectiveness of our experiment on the Patio Pride Peas. We kept the fertilizer amount,
lighting amount, and procedures we used to plant, measure and water consistent
throughout the experiment. This ensured we were able to isolate the impact of the soil
composition on the dependent variables related to the growth of the plant.
Research Question
How do the soil additives biochar and perlite affect the growth and development of Patio
Pride Pea plants compared to 100% lunar regolith?
Hypothesis
If the soil mixture contains biochar as an additive, then plants will have better growth
rates.
1

Variables
Independent Variables
The experiment has two independent variables that will be used to alter the composition
of the regolith in order to test their effect on plant growth. Our first variable is a soil
additive called biochar, which will be tested in experiment two. Biochar will add organic
material and volume to the regolith. The second independent variable is perlite, which
will be tested in experiment one. Perlite will improve aeration and add volume to the
regolith mixture. These specific additives were chosen due to how their specs compared
to our other considerations. These specs can be seen by the chart below.
Dependent Variables
The experiment’s dependent variable is the size and production of the pea plants. The
goal is to determine which soil additive will grow peas most effectively. We will measure
the pea plant’s height in millimeters, number of leaflets, number of blooms, and
number of pods(if applicable). At the conclusion of the experiment, we will also measure
the fresh and dry weight of each pea plant.
We chose to grow the Patio Pride Pea because it reaches maturity within 40 days,
requires a small growing area, and provides a nutritious final product that would be
beneficial to astronauts aboard the International Space Station. The table below contains
information that helped us come to a conclusion about what plant we were going to
grow.

Control
In regards to soil composition, our two control pots will be composed of 100% lunar
regolith. Other variables that will be added at constant rates throughout the experiment
will help provide additional nutrients to the soil and balance the pH value, thus
addressing some of the problems identified in our research while still allowing our team
to test the two independent variables.
Throughout our three test groups, 20 grams of egg shells will be added to each pot to help
adjust the acidic pH of the lunar regolith. A 2-15-15 liquid fertilizer will be applied every
other week to the control, experiment one, and experiment two pots at the same rate.
Because the lunar regolith contains very little nutrients, the addition of fertilizer at equal
rates across our control and both experiments will provide vital nutrients to our seeds,
thus increasing the chances of plant germination and growth, and allowing our team a
better chance to measure plant growth across the entire experimental design.

Soil compositions will be pre-mixed by measuring the volume of each material. Once the
soil compositions are mixed and divided equally between the pots corresponding to our
experimental design, we will follow the procedures below:
1. Moisten soil using 100 ml of water.
2. Create two indentations 1 inch deep in each pot.
3. Place one seed in each indentation (two per pot).
4. Cover lightly with soil.
5. Add an additional 15 ml of water above the location of the seeds.
6. Once all pots are planted, they will be placed evenly under the grow light away
from other light sources.
One week after germination has occurred, plants will be thinned to one plant per pot.
Number of seeds germinating in each pot, along with the days to germination will be
recorded in our data.
Watering Procedure
After the initial moistening of the soil, plants will be checked on Monday, Wednesday,
and Friday for soil moisture. When soil moisture is below 20% in any group (control,
experiment one, or experiment two), 50 ml of water will be added. This protocol will be
followed until germination. From germination until the end of the experiment, each
plant will be given 100 ml of water twice weekly. The amount of water given may be
adjusted throughout the experiment as needed based on the soil moisture content. Any
changes in procedure will be documented in our final report.
Modifications
Modifications were made to the watering procedure during the experiment. These
modifications were attributed to two factors:
-
Inaccurate readings from the soil moisture probe
-
Observed wilting of the plants
One week into our experiment, we implemented a more flexible watering system that
was based on observed moisture content within each experimental group.
Light Procedure
Our only light source will be a plant grow light. We will use a rotating light procedure
where the peas are in full light for 12 hours and in the dark for 12 hours. All of the pots
will be put on the same lighting procedure in order to avoid confounding factors. For this
same reason, all pots will be rotated weekly under the grow light.
Measurement Procedure
4

The plants will be measured every Friday at 9:00 AM to ensure consistency. We will
measure the pea plant’s height in millimeters, number of leaflets, number of blooms,
and size of pea pods in millimeters. A final measurement of fresh and dry weight will
also be recorded for each plant at the conclusion of the experiment.
To ensure accuracy in plant growth measurements, our team will use the following
protocols:
-
Plant Height: Lay one ruler across the top of the planting container. Use another
ruler to measure the height of the plant from the ruler to the last node on the
plant (location of last leaf that is at least 2 ml in length).
-
Number of leaves - Peas have compound leaves. To ensure the most accuracy,
students will count individual leaflets. Any leaflet greater than 2 ml will be
counted.
Additional environmental measurements will include soil’s temperature, water amount,
humidity, and soil PH. Our tools for measuring will be a PH monitor, a humidity monitor,
a scale, and a ruler. These measurements will help our team consider environmental
factors that could affect plant growth that are outside of our independent variables.
All measurement data will be recorded in Google Sheets. All recordings will include the
unit of measurement, team member recording the data, and a date stamp.
Modifications
Due to school closures, some growth data was collected on Thursday or Monday (see
Table 1 and Table 2).

Experimental Design Rationale
This soil composition experimental design will allow us to isolate the independent factors
of biochar and perlite.. We decided to use the addition of egg shells in our pots to
account for the acidic nature of lunar regolith. We also recognized the need for
additional nutrients due to the lack of nutrient availability in the lunar regolith. Because
peas are legumes, we recognized we did not need to focus our efforts on nitrogen.
Instead, we chose the 2-15-15 fertilizer to add the macronutrients phosphorus and
potassium to our soil. Through our research, we identified pH adjustment and lack of
nutrients as major issues that could impact plant growth. By adding the egg shells and
6

fertilizers at an equal rate throughout the three test groups, we can increase the
possibility that our plants will grow while being able to isolate the independent variables
of biochar and perlite.

Qualitative Observations
Throughout this experiment, the team made several qualitative observations related to
the success of the plant growth. These observations helped us make informed decisions
about modifications to our watering procedure and allowed us to better understand our
quantitative data. Here are some of the important observations we recorded throughout
the experiment:
-
The perlite and biochar were both significantly less dense than the lunar regolith,
making it very difficult to mix the soils together. Upon watering, the soils
separated and the biochar and perlite sat on top of the regolith for the remainder
of the experiment.
-
Due to the composition of the biochar and perlite, the seeds and roots were
mainly contained in the top layer of perlite in experiment two and biochar in
experiment three.
-
When watering, experiment 2 appeared to retain the least amount of water, with
water running immediately out of the bottom of the pots. The control group took
the longest time to absorb the water.
-
The plants were extremely fragile, easily breaking during the measuring and
staking processes. Two plants, number 9 and number 3, both broke during the
experiment. Number 3 died as a result and number 9 had stunted growth because
the top of the plant was broken.
Discussion
From the data we have collected during this project, we have seen growth in multiple
ways. As shown in the data most of our plants grew rapidly. Six out of ten of our plants
died (see Figure 3). For plant numbers 1, 3, and 7 the plants were dry when they were
taken away from the table. Numbers 5, 8, and 10 died were still slightly moist. The plants
9

that survived had no buds, but they had a large amount of leaves.
Our quantitative data shows that experiment two had the greatest overall growth,
followed by our control group, and finally experiment three. At the conclusion of the
experiment, average plant height in our perlite group was 57 cm, compared to 52
centimeters in the control group, and 35 cm in the biochar group.
In terms of number of leaflets, results were less clear. At the end of the experiment, our
control group had the highest average number of leaflets. However, we observed all
plants that were still living at that point in the experiment looked similar in terms of
health. These results appear to be inconclusive, as there isn’t a clear experimental group
that performed better than others.
Conclusion
Our initial hypothesis was not supported by the results of this experiment. Experiment
three, testing the effects of biochar as an additive to lunar regolith, showed the least
amount of growth and leaflets at the end of the experiment. Additionally, 75% of plants
in experiment three died.
The results of the experiment support the use of perlite as an additive to lunar regolith to
increase the success of this variety of pea plants. PThe results indicate perlite allows
higher moisture retention in lunar soils, allowing for better plant growth.
Recommendations for Future Research
Based on our results and research, further investigation into the following areas is
recommended: analysis of the impact of fertilizer in 100% lunar regolith soils,
cost-benefit analysis of soil additives like perlite, the impact of lunar regolith on the
hardiness and overall growth rate of peas, effective methods for incorporating additives
into lunar regolith, and nutritional analysis of peas grown in lunar regolith.
